article.title: A random number generator determined the “favorite" in our forecast
article.subtitle: So fine: let's go to the tiebreaker round.

extraction.summary: Silver's final 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential forecast, run at midnight on Election Day with 80,000 simulations instead of the usual 40,000, gave Harris 40,012 Electoral College wins (50.015%). The remaining 39,988 split between Trump (39,718) and 269-269 ties (about 270), and ties would likely be resolved for Trump in the House. Silver explains that Monte Carlo sampling error (about ±0.5 points at 40K and ±0.35 at 80K) is larger than Harris's edge, so the 'favorite' was effectively chosen by the random number generator. He notes that the model's implied popular-vote margin (Harris +2.1) exceeds the national polling average (Harris +1) because it relies mainly on extrapolation from state polls. He reviews the model's record across past cycles, notes how stable the 2024 forecast was, dismisses early voting and internal-poll rumors, and applies his informal '15 clarifying questions' as tiebreakers (8 Harris, 4 Trump, 3 pass), suggesting Harris's 'real' odds might be about 52%.
models_discussed: Allan Lichtman's 13 Keys to the White House

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model normally runs 40,000 simulations per forecast update. For the final Election Day forecast, it was decided in advance to run 80,000 simulations instead.

quantities.name: final run simulation count
quantities.context: final forecast run at midnight on Election Day 2024

findings.rationale: The race was expected to be extremely close, and more simulations reduce sampling error.
findings.evidence_quote: We'd decided ahead of time to run 80,000 simulations instead of our usual 40K.

findings.statement: In the final 2024 Silver Bulletin forecast, Harris won the Electoral College in 40,012 of 80,000 simulations (50.015%). Trump won 39,718, and the remaining simulations (about 270) were 269-269 ties with no majority.
findings.evidence_quote: Kamala Harris won the Electoral College in … 40,012 of them, or 50.015 percent. The remaining 39,988 were split between Trump (39,718) and no majority

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin presidential model reports 269-269 Electoral College ties as a separate 'no majority' outcome rather than awarding them to a candidate. Silver says a tie would in practice probably be resolved for Trump in the U.S. House.
findings.rationale: Contingent House election rules would likely favor Trump.
findings.evidence_quote: no majority — a 269-269 tie — which practically speaking would probably be resolved for Trump in the U.S. House.

findings.statement: Because the Silver Bulletin model is probabilistic (Monte Carlo) rather than deterministic, the reported win probability carries sampling error. The margin of error is about ±0.5 points of win probability at 40,000 simulations and about ±0.35 points at 80,000.
findings.rationale: A finite number of simulations produces sampling noise.
findings.evidence_quote: there's a small amount of error introduced into the model because it's probabilistic rather than deterministic. The margin of error on 40,000 simulations is about ± 0.5 points

findings.statement: A running tally of Harris's win probability over the final 80,000 simulations swung widely early on (roughly 48% to 52% within the first few thousand simulations). It then converged toward 50%, with Harris ahead 50.7%-49.3% after 18,000 simulations before Trump plus ties caught up. The final ordering was decided only around simulations #79,281-#79,603.
findings.rationale: This illustrates how noisy the simulation count is relative to a near-50/50 race.
findings.evidence_quote: Harris jumped out to a huge early lead, ahead 50.7%-49.3% after the 18,000th simulation — but then Trump + no majority mounted a thrilling comeback.

findings.statement: Silver says a 50.015% forecast should not be read as the model predicting a Harris win. The edge is smaller than Monte Carlo error and smaller than the 50.5% empirical frequency of heads in a coin flip, so the 'favorite' was effectively determined by the random number generator.
findings.evidence_quote: the race is literally closer than a coin flip: empirically, heads wins 50.5 percent of the time, more than Harris's 50.015 percent.

findings.statement: Silver says the model's uncertainty is not inflated by a default tendency to hedge or by adding extra uncertainty parameters without reason. He points to past cycles in which the model showed clear favorites.
findings.rationale: The model's record shows clear favorites in most years.
findings.evidence_quote: It's not because my default is to hedge or just throw some extra uncertainty parameters in the model for no reason.

findings.statement: Silver's model track record by cycle: Democrats were clear Electoral College favorites in 2008, 2012 and 2020. Clinton was a slightly less clear favorite in 2016, with the model more bullish on Trump than betting odds and other forecasts. In 2010 Democrats were favored to keep the Senate but lose the House. 2014 was a predictable Republican outcome. In 2018 Democrats were heavy House favorites but big Senate underdogs. In 2022 the final Senate forecast was close but the House forecast was not.
findings.evidence_quote: This is my fifth presidential election — and my ninth general election overall, counting midterms — and there has never been anything like this.

findings.statement: In 2022, Silver's model was bullish on Democrats relative to conventional wisdom and never bought into the 'red wave' narrative.
findings.evidence_quote: we were bullish on Democrats relative to the conventional wisdom and never really bought into the "red wave" narrative

findings.statement: The June 2024 version of the Silver Bulletin model definitively showed Joe Biden as an underdog before Democrats replaced him with Harris.
findings.evidence_quote: the model definitively showed Joe Biden as an underdog

findings.statement: After relaunching with Harris, the 2024 Silver Bulletin forecast was stable: it spent 87 of 98 days within the 60/40 range in one direction or the other. Per the chart, it began around Trump 62% / Harris 38% at launch in late July, peaked near Trump 64% in early September before the Harris-Trump debate, peaked near Harris 58% in late September, and finished at Harris 50.0% / Trump 49.6%.
findings.evidence_quote: the model has spent 87 of 98 days since we relaunched in the 60/40 range in one direction or another.

findings.statement: Silver describes the 2024 race as following a sine-wave-like pattern, with small shifts of momentum roughly every three weeks. He is generally distrustful of 'momentum' because what goes up tends to come back down, but he notes that at the very end of a race there is no time for reversion.
findings.evidence_quote: under most circumstances, I'm actually pretty distrustful of the concept of "momentum" in the context of elections. Because what goes up tends to come right back down

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin model's projected national popular vote margin is largely extrapolated from state polls rather than national polls. In the final 2024 forecast this gave Harris +2.1, versus +1 in the national polling average.
findings.rationale: State polls, including Iowa, were relatively good for Harris.
findings.evidence_quote: The model, however, instead calibrates her popular vote margin at 2.1 points because it's largely based on extrapolations from state polls rather than national polls

findings.statement: Silver says a Harris lead of about 1 point in the national popular vote would probably still leave her an underdog in the Electoral College, implying a Republican-leaning Electoral College bias.
findings.evidence_quote: Harris leads by 1 point in our final national polling average — that probably still leaves her as un underdog in the Electoral College.

findings.statement: In the final 2024 Silver Bulletin polling averages, 6 of the 7 key swing states were within 1.2 points. Arizona, leaning Trump, was the only one with something resembling a clear lead.
findings.evidence_quote: In 6 of the 7 key swing states, our final polling average is within 1.2 points; the only one with something resembling a clear lead is Arizona for Trump.

findings.statement: Late polling may lag real movement because most pollsters conducted their final interviews the week before the election and published over the final weekend. Silver guesses that fresh high-quality polls fielded that weekend would have shown Harris at about 52-53%.

quantities.name: Silver's guessed Harris probability
quantities.context: if fresh polls had been fielded

findings.evidence_quote: most pollsters did their final interviews last week and then published their numbers this weekend and closed up shop

findings.statement: Silver names Selzer, Marist College and NYT/Siena as higher-quality pollsters he trusts not to herd. He contrasts them with 'gutless' pollsters that copy others' results.
findings.rationale: Herding reduces the information value of polls.
findings.evidence_quote: the higher-quality pollsters that I trust not to herd, namely Selzer, Marist College, and for the most part NYT/Siena

findings.statement: Close polls do not necessarily predict a close result. A systematic polling error in either direction (favoring Trump or Harris) remains possible.
findings.evidence_quote: the close polls don't necessarily predict a close result. How there could be another systematic polling error favoring either Trump or Harris

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin coverage enumerates the 128 possible combinations of the 7 swing states (2^7) as 'paths to victory'. The model also treats Nebraska and Maine congressional districts as separate electoral units (NE-2, NE-3, ME-2, etc.).
findings.evidence_quote: guided you through the 128 paths to victory

findings.statement: At typical sportsbook odds, a bettor must win 52.5% of the time to have a +EV bet. A 50.015% model edge is therefore not bettable.
findings.evidence_quote: at the odds sportsbooks typically offer, you have to win 52.5 percent of the time to have a +EV bet.

findings.statement: Silver does not trust gut feelings, early voting data, or rumors of internal polls as election indicators, saying people tend to overweight them.
findings.evidence_quote: I also don't really believe in indicators like early voting or rumors of internal polls that people tend to overweight.

findings.statement: Silver's models have traditionally used a Gallup poll of voter enthusiasm to calibrate the turnout forecast.
findings.evidence_quote: according to the Gallup poll we've traditionally used to calibrate our turnout forecast.

findings.statement: Silver's '15 clarifying questions for close elections' (first written in 2009) are informal tiebreakers outside the model. They cover enthusiasm, turnout operation, the incumbent rule, demographics of undecideds, late coverage, elevator pitch, national environment, early voting, up/downballot effects, hard-to-poll voters, past polling bias, crowd sizes, fundraising, positivity of the campaign, and control of electoral apparatus. Silver says they can move a 50% race to perhaps 52-53%, but not to 55% or 60%.
findings.rationale: These factors matter little and get overweighted, but can break ties.
findings.evidence_quote: They won't get you from 50 percent to 60 percent, or even 55 percent, but maybe they can get you to 52 or 53 if they mostly point in the same direction.

findings.statement: In 2024 the tiebreaker questions came out 8 Harris, 4 Trump and 3 pass. Valuing each at 0.5 points of win probability, Silver suggests Harris's 'real' odds might be about 52%.
findings.evidence_quote: If each one is worth half a percentage point of win probability, then maybe that means Harris's "real" odds are 52 percent

findings.statement: Silver says that, empirically, past polling has systematically underestimated Trump, and that Trump's voters are the harder ones to reach in polls.
findings.evidence_quote: the answer in an empirical sense is obviously Trump.

findings.statement: Many if not most polls in the Silver Bulletin database are conducted online or by other non-phone means. Landline calling is barely needed anymore.
findings.evidence_quote: many if not most of the polls in our database are conducted by the Internet or other means.

findings.statement: Silver argues that Lichtman's 13 Keys, applied strictly as Lichtman applied them in the past, predict Trump rather than Harris. The 'no primary contest' key (#2) should be turned against Democrats because of the Biden replacement fight, which alone flips the call. The 'no social unrest' key (#8) arguably should be turned against Harris as well. The 'strong short-term economy' key (#5) is subjective: Lichtman counted it against Bush in 1992 based on voter perception, and voters feel similarly now.
findings.rationale: Lichtman applies the keys inconsistently and subjectively.
findings.evidence_quote: the "no primary contest" key (#2) should pretty clearly be "turned" against Democrats given the huge fight they had over replacing Biden with Harris, and that alone would change the prediction to Trump.

political_insights.insight: Black and Hispanic voters were considerably more likely than white voters to be undecided late in 2024, which could favor Harris if they 'come home'. In the NYT/Siena October poll, 7% of nonwhite voters were undecided versus 4% of white voters, and 6% of independents versus 2% of partisans. Young voters (18-29) were most often 'probable, not definite' at 25%.
political_insights.evidence: NYT/Siena October national likely voter poll table.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Allocation of undecideds by demographic group can shift late projections.

political_insights.insight: There was evidence of a late Harris rebound with Latino voters, including a Univision poll of Pennsylvania Latinos showing Harris up 64-30. This was better than her earlier crosstabs and better than Biden in 2020, possibly helped by the Madison Square Garden 'Puerto Rico' remark.
political_insights.evidence: Univision poll; Pennsylvania's large Puerto Rican population.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Single-group polls may signal late shifts not captured in topline averages.

political_insights.insight: Worldwide there is an anti-incumbent mood and a conservative shift, especially on immigration, which favors Trump.
The 'incumbent rule' is ambiguous in 2024: Trump was a former president, while Harris was the incumbent vice president.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Incumbency variables need care when candidates do not fit standard categories.

political_insights.insight: Abortion referendums in Nevada and Arizona and Mark Robinson's candidacy in North Carolina may help Harris.
Slightly more Democrats than Republicans voted early in party-registration states, with margins down from 2020. Silver says 2020 is a poor comparison because of COVID.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Early vote comparisons to 2020 are confounded.

political_insights.insight: Fundraising may now be underweighted after an overcorrection, though top-of-ticket candidates have more money than they need. Harris led strongly on fundraising.

open_questions: How the model translates state polls into a national popular vote estimate (the +2.1 vs. +1 discrepancy).
How exactly the Gallup enthusiasm poll enters the turnout forecast.
What random seed or simulation procedure is used, and whether multiple runs are averaged.
How undecided voters are allocated by demographics in the model, if at all.
